ref: 21.11 (Latin Library section [11]; ANF ch. 21, paragraph 'Cleanthes ... Spirit')
latin: [11] Et nos autem sermoni atque rationi itemque virtuti, per quae omnia molitum deum ediximus, propriam substantiam spiritum inscribimus, cui et sermo insit pronuntianti et ratio adsit disponenti et virtus praesit perficienti. Hunc ex deo prolatum didicimus et prolatione generatum et idcirco filium dei et deum dictum ex unitate substantiae; nam et deus spiritus.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); cross-checked against archive.org patrologiaecur01mign (Migne PL 1, OCR) (Latin 'Hunc ex Deo prolatum ... ex unitate substantiae' matches; column about 458, approximate)
english: Cleanthes ascribes all this to spirit, which he maintains pervades the universe. And we, in like manner, hold that the Word, and Reason, and Power, by which we have said God made all, have spirit as their proper and essential substratum, in which the Word has in being to give forth utterances, and reason abides to dispose and arrange, and power is over all to execute. We have been taught that He proceeds forth from God, and in that procession He is generated; so that He is the Son of God, and is called God from unity of substance with God. For God, too, is a Spirit.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Word, Reason and Power are given the proper substance 'spirit', that the Word proceeds from God and is generated by that procession, and is therefore called Son and God from unity of substance.
limits: The 'spirit' here is the substance of the Logos as God's creative Word, not a separate Holy Spirit. The passage is a Stoic-style analogy (Cleanthes' pneuma) and says nothing about the Spirit as a third person. Generation by 'prolatio' is the point opponents press (Prax. 7 is outside this assignment).

ref: 21.12 (Latin Library section [12]; ANF ch. 21, paragraph 'Even when the ray')
latin: [12] Et cum radius ex sole porrigitur, portio ex summa; sed sol erit in radio, quia solis est radius nec separatur substantia sed extenditur, [ita de spiritu spiritus et de deo deus] ut lumen de lumine accensum. Manet integra et indefecta materia[e] matrix, etsi plures inde traduces qualitatis mutueris.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); Migne PL 1 OCR prints the bracketed clause unbracketed ('de Spiritu Spiritus, et de Deo Deus, ut lumen de lumine accensum')
english: Even when the ray is shot from the sun, it is still part of the parent mass; the sun will still be in the ray, because it is a ray of the sun — there is no division of substance, but merely an extension. Thus Christ is Spirit of Spirit, and God of God, as light of light is kindled. The material matrix remains entire and unimpaired, though you derive from it any number of shoots possessed of its qualities;
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: The sun-ray image shows that the Son remains of one substance with the Father while extended from Him, 'light of light'.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (unity of substance; derivation without division)
limits: The clause 'de spiritu spiritus et de deo deus' is in square brackets in the Latin Library text (editorial doubt marker); ANF translates it without any note. The analogy 'ray from the sun' is the classic derivation image that Praxeas-type and Arian critics read as partition or subordination.

ref: 21.13 (Latin Library section [13]; ANF ch. 21, paragraph 'so, too, that which has come forth')
latin: [13] Ita et quod de deo profectum est, deus et dei filius et unus ambo; ita et de spiritu spiritus et de deo deus modulo alter[num], numerum gradu, non statu fecit, et a matrice non recessit, sed excessit.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur01mign (Migne PL 1, OCR) OCR matches 'modulo alternum, numerum gradu, non statu'
english: so, too, that which has come forth out of God is at once God and the Son of God, and the two are one. In this way also, as He is Spirit of Spirit and God of God, He is made a second in manner of existence— in position, not in nature; and He did not withdraw from the original source, but went forth.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says that what came from God is both God and the Son of God, and that as 'Spirit of Spirit and God of God' the Son is a second in mode of existence, not in nature.
use: answer to objection (the 'second' / secundus objection) and supports Trinitarian reading
limits: 'Second' is explicitly said to be 'in position, not in nature' (gradu, non statu), so it is a subordination of order, not of substance. Opponents will read 'secundus' as creaturely subordination; this sentence is the local answer, not a full Nicene formula.

latin: Vnum omnino Deum esse nec alium praeter mundi conditorem qui uniuersa de nihilo produxerit per uerbum suum primo omnium emissum. [3] Id uerbum filium eius appellatum in nomine Dei uarie uisum a patriarchis, in prophetis semper auditum, postremo delatum ex spiritu patris Dei et uirtute in uirginem Mariam, carnem factum in utero eius et ex ea natum egisse Iesum Christum.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim) (Latin Library capitalisation kept: 'Vnum'); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR: 'unum omnino Deum esse, nec alium praeter mundi Conditorem; qui universa de nihilo produxerit, per Verbum suum primo omnium emissum' and 'Filium ejus appellatum' found (column about 31-32, approximate)
english: that which prescribes the belief that there is one only God, and that He is none other than the Creator of the world, who produced all things out of nothing through His own Word, first of all sent forth; that this Word is called His Son, and, under the name of God, was seen in diverse manners by the patriarchs, heard at all times in the prophets, at last brought down by the Spirit and Power of the Father into the Virgin Mary, was made flesh in her womb, and, being born of her, went forth as Jesus Christ;
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read; the 1918 reprint (antenicenefather03robe) gives the same page 249
what_it_says: Tertullian's summary of the rule of faith names one God the Creator, the Word sent forth first and called His Son, brought down by the Spirit and Power of the Father into Mary, and the Father at the right hand; it sends the Holy Ghost as the Power that leads believers.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Father, Son and Spirit all present in the rule); the Spirit is 'the Power sent instead of Christ' and 'of the Father', not explicitly a co-equal person
limits: The rule is stated in economic terms (Word 'sent forth' and 'brought down'); the Spirit appears as 'ex spiritu patris Dei et uirtute' and as 'uicariam uim spiritus sancti' sent by Christ, which an Arian reads as a subordinate power. The phrase 'unum omnino Deum' is the ground Praxeas and modern modalists also claim.

latin: unicum quidem deum credimus, sub hac tamen dispensatione, quam oi0konomi/an dicimus, ut unici dei sit et filius, sermo ipsius qui ex ipso processerit, per quem omnia facta sunt et sine quo factum est nihil: hunc missum a patre in virginem et ex ea natum hominem et deum, filium hominis et filium dei, et cognominatum Iesum Christum: hunc passum, hunc mortuum et sepultum secundum scripturas, et resuscitatum a patre et in caelo resumptum sedere ad dexteram patris venturum iudicare vivos et mortuos: qui exinde miserit, secundum promissionem suam, a patre spiritum sanctum paracletum, sanctificatorem fidei eorum qui credunt in patrem et filium et spiritum sanctum.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); cross-checked against archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) ('unicum quidem Deum credimus', 'Patrem et Filium et Spiritum sanctum' found in OCR, col. 179-180 approx.)
english: believe that there is one only God, but under the following dispensation, or οἰκονομία, as it is called, that this one only God has also a Son, His Word, who proceeded from Himself, by whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. Him we believe to have been sent by the Father into the Virgin, and to have been born of her — being both Man and God, the Son of Man and the Son of God, and to have been called by the name of Jesus Christ; we believe Him to have suffered, died, and been buried, according to the Scriptures, and, after He had been raised again by the Father and taken back to heaven, to be sitting at the right hand of the Father, and that He will come to judge the quick and the dead; who sent also from heaven from the Father, according to His own promise, the Holy Ghost, the Paraclete, the sanctifier of the faith of those who believe in the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Ghost.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: The rule of faith names one God, the Son (Word sent from God and born of the Virgin), and the Holy Spirit sent by the Father, and ends in the formula 'Father, Son and Holy Spirit'.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (explicit triad in the rule)
limits: The Latin is the rule as Tertullian quotes it; the sentence is a summary, not a creed, and the 'oikonomia' clause qualifies how the one God 'has also a Son'. Modalists such as Praxeas accepted the names but denied distinct persons, so the triad alone does not settle the question.

latin: quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens patrem et filium et spiritum, tres autem non statu sed gradu, nec substantia sed forma, nec potestate sed specie, unius autem substantiae et unius status et unius potestatis, quia unus deus ex quo et gradus isti et formae et species in nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti deputantur.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR: 'tres dirigens, Patrem, et Filium, et Spiritum sanctum. Tres autem non statu, sed gradu'
english: which distributes the Unity into a Trinity, placing in their order the three Persons— the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power, inasmuch as He is one God, from whom these degrees and forms and aspects are reckoned, under the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says the economy distributes the Unity into a Trinity of three Persons, 'three not in condition but in degree, not in substance but in form, not in power but in aspect', of one substance, condition and power.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (distinction without division); also an answer to objections that 'gradus' means separate beings
limits: Tertullian's terms (gradus, forma, species, statu) are not Nicene terms (hypostasis / ousia / homoousios); scholars disagree on whether 'gradus' expresses a real distinction of persons (Hanson's critique is the usual objection; not checked in this run). The 'degree' wording is what an Arian critic would press as subordination.

latin: Regula quidem fidei una omnino est, sola immobilis et irreformabilis, credendi scilicet in uni cum deum omnipotentem, mundi conditorem, et filium eius Iesum Christum, natum ex virgine Maria, crucifixum sub Pontio Pilato, tertia die resuscitatum a mortuis, receptum in caelis, sedentem nunc ad dexteram patris, venturum iudi care vivos et mortuos per camis etiam resurrectionem.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim) (typo 'camis' for 'carnis' in the Latin Library text, kept as printed); Migne PL 2 OCR contains 'Una omnino est, sola immobilis et irreformabilis' (column not read)
english: The rule of faith, indeed, is altogether one, alone immoveable and irreformable; the rule, to wit, of believing in one only God omnipotent, the Creator of the universe, and His Son Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised again the third day from the dead, received in the heavens, sitting now at the right (hand) of the Father, destined to come to judge quick and dead through the resurrection of the flesh as well (as of the spirit).
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4 (Roberts & Donaldson, New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, 1913), archive.org antenicenefather04robe, PDF page read with pdftotext
what_it_says: This rule of faith names only one God the Creator, His Son Jesus Christ with his birth, passion and return, and the resurrection of the flesh; it does not name the Holy Spirit.
use: objection (a rule of faith without the Spirit) and answer (the Spirit is named later as the Paraclete who leads into truth, 1.6)
limits: The ANF adds '(as of the spirit)' in brackets after 'resurrection of the flesh'; this gloss is not in the Latin. The Latin says 'per carnis etiam resurrectionem' only. Opponents cite the omission; defenders note 1.6 'vicario domini, spiritu sancto'.

latin: Nunc et simplicius respondeamus. non competebat ex semine humano dei filium nasci, ne si totus esset filius hominis non esset et dei filius nihilque haberet amplius Salomone et amplius Iona, ut de Hebionis opinione credendus erat. ergo iam dei filius ex patris dei semine, id est spiritu, [2] ut esset et hominis filius caro ei sola erat ex hominis carne sumenda sine viri semine: vacabat enim semen viri apud habentem dei semen. itaque sicut nondum natus ex virgine patrem deum habere potuit sine homine matre, aeque cum de virgine nasceretur potuit matrem habere hominem sine homine patre: [3] sic denique homo cum deo dum caro hominis cum spiritu dei, caro sine semine ex homine, spiritus cum semine ex deo.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR: 'ex Patris Dei semine' found
english: Now, that we may give a simpler answer, it was not fit that the Son of God should be born of a human father's seed, lest, if He were wholly the Son of a man, He should fail to be also the Son of God, and have nothing more than a Solomon or a Jonas, Matthew 12:41-42 — as Ebion thought we ought to believe concerning Him. In order, therefore, that He who was already the Son of God— of God the Father's seed, that is to say, the Spirit — might also be the Son of man, He only wanted to assume flesh, of the flesh of man without the seed of a man; for the seed of a man was unnecessary for One who had the seed of God. As, then, before His birth of the virgin, He was able to have God for His Father without a human mother, so likewise, after He was born of the virgin, He was able to have a woman for His mother without a human father. He is thus man with God, in short, since He is man's flesh with God's Spirit — flesh (I say) without seed from man, Spirit with seed from God.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son of God is of God's seed, that is the Spirit, and that the flesh of Christ came from the virgin without human seed: 'flesh without seed from man, Spirit with seed from God'.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Son as Spirit from God) and is the text anti-Trinitarians cite as 'Son derived from God's seed'
limits: The seed/Spirit language is about the Son's divine origin in the Incarnation argument; it is not a systematic doctrine of eternal generation. ANF chapter title itself calls the Son 'the Spirit' here, which critics cite against a distinct Person.

latin: idoneus enim non erat dei filius qui solus hominem liberaret, a solo et singulari serpente deiectum? ergo iam non unus deus nec unus salutificator, sed duo salutis artifices, et utique alter altero indigens.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR: 'Ergo jam non unus Deus, nec unus salutificator, si duo salutis artifices, et utique alter altero indigens' found
english: The Son of God, in truth, was not competent alone to deliver man, whom a solitary and single serpent had overthrown! There is, then, no longer but one God, but one Saviour, if there be two to contrive salvation, and one of them in need of the other.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian argues against Marcion's angel-saviour that there cannot be two saviours, one needing the other, so there is only one God and one Saviour.
use: answer to objection (monotheism against two-gods charge; Marcionite dualism)
limits: This is an argument against a two-God or angel-mediator model, not a statement about Father, Son and Spirit. Opponents read 'the Son of God ... not competent alone' as a limit on the Son's power.

latin: An hae sunt pusillitates, quae iam hinc praeiudicare debebunt Christum humanis passionibus obiectum eius dei esse cui humanitates exprobrantur a vobis? Nam et profitemur Christum semper egisse in dei patris nomine, ipsum ab initio conversatum, ipsum congressum cum patriarchis et prophetis, filium creatoris, sermonem eius, quena ex semetipso proferendo filium fecit, et exinde omni dispositioni suae voluntatique praefecit, diminuens illum modico citra angelos, sicut apud David scriptum est;
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim) (Latin Library has 'quena' for 'quem', printed as in the source; Migne PL 2 OCR reads 'quem ex semetipso proferendo filium fecit'); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) cross-check matched
english: Are these the humiliations which henceforth are to raise a prejudice against Christ (the subject as He is of human passions ) being a partaker of that Godhead against which you make the participation in human qualities a reproach? Now we believe that Christ did ever act in the name of God the Father; that He actually from the beginning held intercourse with (men); actually communed with patriarchs and prophets; was the Son of the Creator; was His Word; whom God made His Son by emitting Him from His own self, and thenceforth set Him over every dispensation
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son is the Creator's Word, whom God made His Son by emitting Him from Himself and set over every dispensation, and that Christ acted always in the Father's name.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Word as Son, sent from the Father) and is the prolatio text Arians cite (God 'made' the Son)
limits: 'Quem ex semetipso proferendo filium fecit' is the sentence most used against eternal generation ('God made the Son'). It is an argument against Marcion, not a definition of the Trinity.

latin: Ipse enim et veteri testamento pronuntiarat, Deum nemo videbit et vivet, patrem invisibilem determinans, in cuius auctoritate et nomine ipse erat deus qui videbatur, dei filius.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR: 'Patrem invisibilem determinans, in cujus auctoritate ... dei filius' found
english: He means that the Father is invisible, in whose authority and in whose name was He God who appeared as the Son of God.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian explains that the Father is invisible and the God who was seen and heard was the Son acting in the Father's authority and name.
use: answer to objection (invisible/visible distinction: 'the Father never seen, the Son seen')
limits: This is the Father/Son invisibility distinction used against modalism and against Marcion; it does not address the Holy Spirit. Critics say the 'Son as the God who appeared' is an Old Testament theophany identified with the Word.

latin: Igitur si creatoris est imago (ille enim Christum sermonem suum intuens hominem futurum, Faciamus, inquit, hominem ad imaginem et similitudinem nostram)
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR confirms the chapter opening 'Caput viri Christus est' only; the parenthesis was not found in the OCR
english: Since then he is the image of the Creator (for He, when looking on Christ His Word, who was to become man, said, Let us make man in our own image, after our likeness Genesis 1:26)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says God, looking on Christ His Word who was to become man, said 'Let us make man in our image', so the Word is addressed in Genesis 1:26.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (plural 'nostram' read as Word addressed by the Creator)
limits: Tertullian's point is about the image of God and Marcion's Christ; the plural in Genesis is glossed as 'the Word', not as the Spirit or a plurality of persons. Pre-Nicene critics note the gloss is a single reading.

latin: Nam qui ad Moysen loquebatur, ipse erat dei filius qui et semper videbatur; deum enim patrem nemo umquam vidit et vixit. [23] Et ideo constat ipsum dei filium Moyseo esse locutum et dixisse ad populum: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur02mign (Migne PL 2, OCR) OCR: 'ipse erat Dei Filius, qui et semper videbatur' found
english: For He who ever spoke to Moses was the Son of God Himself; who, too, was always seen. Numbers 12:5-8 For God the Father none ever saw, and lived. And accordingly it is agreed that the Son of God Himself spoke to Moses, and said to the people, Behold, I send mine angel before your— that is, the people's — face
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son of God, who was always seen, was the one who spoke to Moses, because God the Father was never seen, and that the Son sent the angel.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Son as the visible divine Speaker of the Old Testament) and answers the Jewish objection that God the Father cannot be seen
limits: Tertullian identifies the Speaker with the Son (a common patristic reading, not checked against other authors in this run). Anti-Trinitarians say it treats the Son as a second visible God and that 'the Son of God' in Exodus is only an angel.

latin: Dicendo autem Patrem Deum quoque cognominamus. Appellatio ista et pietatis et potestatis est. [5] Item in Patre Filius inuocatur. Ego enim, inquit, et Pater unum sumus. [6] Ne mater quidem Ecclesia praeteritu, siquidem in filio et patre mater recognoscitur, de qua constat et patris et filii nomen.

english: Moreover, in saying Father, we also call Him God. That appellation is one both of filial duty and of power. Again, in the Father the Son is invoked; for I, says He, and the Father are One. John 10:30 Nor is even our mother the Church passed by, if, that is, in the Father and the Son is recognized the mother, from whom arises the name both of Father and of Son.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says that in the Father the Son is invoked, quoting 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30), and that the Church is recognised as mother in the Father and the Son.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Father and Son in one name and worship)
limits: The text is about the form of prayer, and uses John 10:30 as a unity-of-will proof; it does not define Father-Son identity of substance or mention the Spirit in this paragraph.

latin: Nomen Dei Patris nemini proditum est. Etiam qui de ipso interrogauerat Moyses, aliud quidem nomen audierat. Nobis reuelatum est in Filio. Et quis enim filius non patris nomen est? Ego ueni, inquit, in nomine Patris et rursus, Pater, glorifica nomen tuum et apertius: Nomen tuum manifestaui hominibus.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); Migne PL 1 OCR did not match the sentence
english: The name of God the Father had been published to none. Even Moses, who had interrogated Him on that very point, had heard a different name. Exodus 3:13-16 To us it has been revealed in the Son, for the Son is now the Father's new name. I have come, says He, in the Father's name; John 5:43 and again, Father, glorify Your name; John 12:28 and more openly, I have manifested Your name to men.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Roberts & Donaldson, Buffalo: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1885), archive.org antenicenefather03robeuoft, djvu OCR text read
what_it_says: Tertullian says the name of the Father was revealed in the Son, who is 'the Father's new name', and quotes John 5:43 and 17:6.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Son reveals the Father's name)
limits: Calling the Son 'the Father's name' is an economic, revelatory statement; anti-Trinitarians read 'name' as an office rather than nature.

ref: 2.3 (Latin Library III.4; ANF Book II chapter 3)
latin: aeque, demonstrantes elementa deos non esse, ad illam agnatorum speciem praestruemus iure deos non esse defendi, quorum parentes, id est elementa, dei non sint. [4] Scimus deum de deo nasci, quemadmodum de non deo non deum.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com (no edition named on the page; Latin Library text read verbatim); archive.org patrologiaecur01mign (Migne PL 1, OCR) OCR matches 'deum de deo nasci, quemadmodum de non deo non deum' (garbled OCR, verified by eye)
english: It is a settled point that a god is born of a god, and that what lacks divinity is born of what is not divine.
page: 131 (1918 reprint OCR; the 1885 OCR page header for this passage could not be read)

what_it_says: Tertullian states the general principle that a god is born of a god, and that what lacks divinity is born of what is not divine, used against pagan gods born from the elements.
use: this is the only Latin source for the wording 'Deum de Deo' that the brief asked for; it is not in Apologeticum 21
limits: The sentence concerns pagan gods and the elements, not the Son; it is the closest Latin wording to the brief's 'Deum de Deo', and it is not 'ut lumen de lumine', which is Apol. 21.12.
